title: Relationship Between Two Circles
statement:
You are given `q` descriptions of two circles in the plane. Each description is six integers `x1 y1 r1 x2 y2 r2`: the centre and radius of the first circle followed by the centre and radius of the second circle. For each description, tell how the two circles relate to each other.

Print exactly one of these words per description, using the first rule that applies:

- `Concentric` if both circles have the same centre (this includes identical circles).
- `Separate` if the circles share no point and neither lies inside the other (the distance between the centres is greater than `r1 + r2`).
- `Touching` if the circles meet at exactly one point, either externally (distance equals `r1 + r2`) or internally (distance equals `|r1 - r2|`).
- `Contained` if one circle lies strictly inside the other without touching it and the centres differ (distance less than `|r1 - r2|`).
- `Intersecting` otherwise: the circles cross at exactly two points.

All inputs are integers, so you can decide every case exactly by comparing squared distances, without floating-point arithmetic.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the integer `q`.
Each of the next `q` lines contains six integers `x1 y1 r1 x2 y2 r2`.
outputFormat: Print `q` lines. Line `i` is one of `Concentric`, `Separate`, `Touching`, `Contained`, `Intersecting`, for the `i`-th description.

examples.explanation: The first pair shares the centre (0, 0). In the second the centres are 5 apart and the radii sum to 5, so the circles touch externally. In the third the centres are 10 apart, more than 2 + 3, so the circles are separate.

Case 1: distance 4 lies strictly between |5 - 3| = 2 and 5 + 3 = 8, so the circles cross. Case 2: distance 1 is less than |10 - 2| = 8, so the small circle is inside the big one. Case 3: distance 2 equals |5 - 3|, so the circles touch internally.

hints: Compute the squared distance between the centres: d2 = (x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2. No square root is needed.
Compare d2 with (r1 + r2)^2 and with (r1 - r2)^2. Squares preserve the order because all of these quantities are non-negative.
Handle the equal-centres case first, then check the cases from the farthest configuration to the nearest.
